analysis.one_liner: Makes drug makers rebate Medicare when Part B drug prices rise faster than inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died at the end of the 116th Congress with four sponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require drug manufacturers to pay Medicare a rebate each quarter for single-source drugs and biologics covered under Medicare Part B (drugs given in a doctor's office, like cancer treatments) if the drug's price has risen faster than general inflation since 2015. The rebates would go into the Medicare trust fund, and seniors' 20% coinsurance on those drugs would be recalculated based on the inflation-adjusted price instead of the inflated price, lowering out-of-pocket costs. Manufacturers that failed to pay the rebate would face a civil penalty of at least 125% of the amount owed.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who use Part B drugs — often expensive physician-administered drugs like cancer treatments and biologics. Their coinsurance would be based on the inflation-adjusted price, and the Medicare trust fund would recapture money from manufacturers whose prices outpaced inflation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare Part B drugs

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to pay Medicare a quarterly rebate on single-source Part B drugs whose prices rose faster than inflation measured against a 2015 benchmark, and deposits those rebates into the Medicare trust fund [S3].
Caps a beneficiary's coinsurance on rebated drugs at 20% of the inflation-adjusted payment amount rather than the full inflated price, directly lowering seniors' out-of-pocket costs [S3].
Gives the Secretary authority to reduce or waive the rebate for drugs on the shortage list, and directs a study of extending the rebate to multiple-source drugs and Medicare Advantage drugs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of single-source drugs and biologics covered under Part B, which would owe rebates whenever their prices outpace inflation, plus a civil money penalty of at least 125% of the owed amount for noncompliance.

drawbacks.text: The rebate only penalizes increases after a fixed 2015 benchmark price, so manufacturers could avoid it by launching new drugs at very high initial prices; the bill's own structure exempts price levels, not just increases [S3].

The bill exempts drugs on the shortage list, which could give manufacturers an incentive to supply drugs thinly or invoke 'exigent circumstances' to escape rebates; the Secretary must adjudicate those cases [S3].

Rebates apply only to single-source drugs over a $100 per-person annual cost threshold and exclude vaccines, packaged units, dialysis drugs, and drugs already subject to 340B or Medicaid rebates, leaving many Part D and multi-source drugs out until a future study and rulemaking [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core mechanism — returning to Medicare the money seniors and taxpayers pay when a drug's price rises faster than inflation — is straightforward and the coinsurance cap gives beneficiaries immediate relief. The main honest critique is that it only disciplines price increases from a 2015 base, not high launch prices, and its carve-outs leave gaps, but those are design limits rather than costs borne by the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and to the Health Subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on October 11, 2019, with three Democratic cosponsors [S3][S4].

The same day it was introduced, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and to the Health Subcommittee, and the record shows no further action through the end of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of single-source Part B drugs, who remain free to raise prices faster than inflation with no rebate owed to Medicare; the bill's low support meant it was never seriously in play.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it, but with only four sponsors and no vote ever scheduled, no meaningful partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Single-source prescription drug and biologic manufacturers
industries.note: These firms would owe quarterly rebates to Medicare whenever Part B drug prices rose faster than inflation, plus a 125% penalty for nonpayment. Because the bill died, they avoid that liability and keep pricing power over physician-administered drugs seniors use.

industries.industry: Specialty pharmacies and physician practices that administer Part B drugs
industries.note: Their revenue tracks Part B payment amounts, so lower inflation-adjusted payment benchmarks and coinsurance changes could trim margins on high-priced biologics, though the bill does not directly change what practices are paid for administration.
